\section[la alegría]{la alegría — joy, happiness}

\label{lesson:ES-C704-alegria}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to seem, then the Spanish for to keep.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la alegría}
\textbf{la alegría} — \textquotedblleft{}joy, happiness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tu visita es una alegría.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Your visit is a joy.}
\end{quote}

\emph{¡Qué alegría!} — How lovely! It is built on \emph{alegre}, cheerful.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{alegría} is built on \emph{alegre} \textquotedblleft{}cheerful\textquotedblright{}, which is usually traced to Latin \emph{alacer} \textquotedblleft{}lively, brisk\textquotedblright{} through a spoken form \emph{alecrem}; English \emph{alacrity} comes from the same Latin word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la alegría}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la alegría}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la alegría}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to seem, then the Spanish for to keep, then say \emph{la alegría} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la alegría mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Joy, happiness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la melancolía]{la melancolía — melancholy, gloom}

\label{lesson:ES-C704-melancolia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to keep, then the Spanish for joy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la melancolía}
\textbf{la melancolía} — \textquotedblleft{}melancholy, gloom\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El otoño me da melancolía.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Autumn makes me melancholy.}
\end{quote}

A soft, lasting sadness. The adjective is \emph{melancólico}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{melancolía} is a learned borrowing from Late Latin \emph{melancholia}, from Greek \emph{melankholía} \textquotedblleft{}blackness of the bile\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{mélas} \textquotedblleft{}black\textquotedblright{} and \emph{khol\'{\={e}}} \textquotedblleft{}bile\textquotedblright{}; old medicine blamed gloom on black bile.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la melancolía}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la melancolía}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la melancolía}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to keep, then the Spanish for joy, then say \emph{la melancolía} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la melancolía mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Melancholy, gloom\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la dicha]{la dicha — happiness, good fortune}

\label{lesson:ES-C704-dicha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for joy, then the Spanish for melancholy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la dicha}
\textbf{la dicha} — \textquotedblleft{}happiness, good fortune\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
¡Qué dicha verte otra vez!
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{What joy to see you again!}
\end{quote}

More literary than \emph{la alegría}. \emph{Nunca es tarde si la dicha es buena} — better late than never.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dicha} is inherited from Latin \emph{dicta} \textquotedblleft{}things said\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{dīcere} \textquotedblleft{}to say\textquotedblright{}; the usual reading is that good fortune was what fate had said for you.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la dicha}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la dicha}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la dicha}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for joy, then the Spanish for melancholy, then say \emph{la dicha} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la dicha mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Happiness, good fortune\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[emocionarse]{emocionarse — to be moved, to get emotional}

\label{lesson:ES-C704-emocionarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for melancholy, then the Spanish for happiness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: emocionarse}
\textbf{emocionarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to be moved, to get emotional\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi madre se emociona con las bodas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My mother gets emotional at weddings.}
\end{quote}

Reflexive: \emph{me emociono}, \emph{te emocionas}. It is about being touched, not about being angry.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{emocionarse} is built on \emph{emoción}, which came from French \emph{émotion} (EtymDB); the French word goes back to Latin \emph{ēmovēre} \textquotedblleft{}to move out, to stir up\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{movēre} \textquotedblleft{}to move\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{emocionarse}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{emocionarse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{emocionarse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for melancholy, then the Spanish for happiness, then say \emph{emocionarse} again
\end{itemize}

\section[llorar]{llorar — to cry, to weep}

\label{lesson:ES-C704-llorar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for happiness, then the Spanish for to be moved.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: llorar}
\textbf{llorar} — \textquotedblleft{}to cry, to weep\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El bebé llora por la noche.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The baby cries at night.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Llorar de alegría} — to cry with joy.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{llorar} is inherited from Latin \emph{plōrāre} \textquotedblleft{}to wail, to weep aloud\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB). Latin \emph{pl-} at the start of a word became \emph{ll-} in Spanish, the same change that turned \emph{plēnus} into \emph{lleno}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for happiness, then the Spanish for to be moved, then say \emph{llorar} again
